property_summary: For any interfaceId, the correct contract returns true whenever super.supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true for IERC1155 or IERC1155MetadataURI (i.e., it reports support for those interfaces), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns false for those interface ids, so there exists an interfaceId (specifically IERC1155 or IERC1155MetadataURI) for which supportsInterface differs.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) must return true whenever interfaceId equals IERC1155 or IERC1155MetadataURI (the reference reports support for those interfaces); the mutant negates those checks and will return false for at least one of those interface ids.

For any bytes4 interfaceId the correct contract returns true when asked about IERC1155 or IERC1155MetadataURI interface ids (it reports support); the mutant negates those checks and will return false for at least one of those interface ids, so there exists an interfaceId where supportsInterface differs.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, the reference C reports support (returns true) for the IERC1155MetadataURI interface id when queried via supportsInterface, whereas the mutant incorrectly returns false for that interface id (so there exists an interface id — IERC1155MetadataURI — where supportsInterface differs).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true whenever interfaceId equals type(IERC1155).interfaceId or type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId (the reference exposes those interfaces); the mutant flips those checks and will return false for at least one of those interface ids, so querying supportsInterface with a fuzzed interfaceId that equals either of those two should always be true on the reference but is false on the mutant for that matching id.

For every interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true for IERC1155MetadataURI.interfaceId when queried (i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) == true), but the mutant that omits IERC1155MetadataURI will return false for that interface id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C returns true for IERC1155MetadataURI.interfaceId (i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) is true) while the mutant that omits IERC1155MetadataURI will return false for that specific interface id, so the universal rule is: c.supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) must succeed (not revert) and return true for all inputs — the mutant breaks this by returning false for that interface id.

For any bytes4 interfaceId input, the correct contract C never reverts when supportsInterface(interfaceId) is called, and specifically it returns true for the IERC1155MetadataURI interface id while the mutant returns false for that id; the test fuzzes an arbitrary bytes4 and asserts that when the interfaceId equals type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId then supportsInterface returns true (the mutant will return false for that input).

For any bytes4 interfaceId input, calling c.supportsInterface(interfaceId) must succeed (not revert) and in particular when interfaceId == type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId the reference returns true while the mutant (which omitted IERC1155MetadataURI) will return false, so the property: supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) == true always holds for the reference and is violated by the mutant.

For any bytes4 input, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) must NOT revert; in particular, for the IERC1155MetadataURI interface id the reference always returns true while the mutant (which omitted that check) will return false for that specific id, so the property is that supportsInterface(type(IERC1155MetadataURI).interfaceId) returns true (and call succeeds) for all inputs — the mutant violates this.

For any address and token id, the reference contract never reverts on balanceOf and returns the stored balance, whereas the mutant will revert for any non-zero address (only allowing the zero address) causing a mismatch or revert for many inputs.

For any non-zero account and any token id, C.balanceOf(account,id) returns the stored balance (which can be non-zero); the mutant always returns 0 so there exist inputs where the returned value differs (non-zero stored balances become zero).

For any account != address(0) and any token id, if the contract reports a nonzero balance for that account/id after minting, balanceOf(account,id) > 0; the mutant always returns 0 so after minting some positive amount the mutant will break this rule.

For any non-zero account and token id, if a caller mints a positive quantity of token id to that account via C.mint, then C.balanceOf(account, id) returns a value >= the minted quantity (reference preserves stored balances; mutant that always returns 0 will violate this for some inputs).

For any non-zero account and any token id within bounds, balanceOf(account,id) returns the stored balance for that exact id; the mutant returns the balance for id+1 so it can differ for some id (e.g. when balances[id] != balances[id+1]).
For any account and id, balanceOf(account, id) returns the stored balance for that exact id; the mutant returns balance for id+1 so there exists an id/account where those balances differ.

For every account and token id, balanceOf(account,id) returns the stored balance for that exact id (i.e. equal to getAllowanceRemaining's pattern doesn't matter) — the mutant returns the balance for id+1 causing balanceOf to differ for some account/id when _balances[id][account] != _balances[id+1][account].

For any account and token id, balanceOf(account,id) always returns the stored balance for that account and id; the mutant incorrectly returns the caller's balance instead, so for some (account, id) where caller != account and their balances differ the mutant will return a different value.

For any owner address A and token id i, calling c.balanceOf(A,i) returns the balance held by A for token i; the mutant instead returns the balance of the caller, so when caller != A and their balances differ the mutant will return a different value.

For any owner address and tokenId, calling c.balanceOf(owner, tokenId) returns the balance for that owner and tokenId (the reference returns _balances[id][owner]); the mutant instead returns the caller's balance causing a mismatch when caller != owner and their balances differ.

For any owner and tokenId, calling c.balanceOf(owner, tokenId) returns the stored balance for that owner and tokenId; the mutant instead returns the caller's balance, so when caller != owner and their balances differ the mutant will return a different value.

For any owner address and tokenId, calling c.balanceOf(owner, tokenId) returns the balance stored for that owner and tokenId (the reference returns _balances[id][owner]); the mutant incorrectly returns the caller's balance, so when the caller is a different address with a different balance the mutant will return a different value.
